new_statements.quote: 慣用ではアクセントを表記することはしないが，ここでは，高く発音される母音の上に´をつけ，低く発音される母音には何もつけない，という形であらわし分ける。なお，アクセントを捨象した表記は下線をひいてこれを示す。アクセント表示においては，子音（または子音＋w/y）をC，母音をV，子音前鼻音をNであらわす。また，任意の音素列をXであらわし，X́は，そのXに含まれるすべての母音が高いことをあらわす。何もつかないXはそのすべての母音が低いことを示す。Nは高い母音の直後でのみ高く発音されるので，高く発音される場合でも´はつけない。 [p. 2] ... 一般にこの言語では，たとえば§2-1-1〜5のA型動詞について述べるような場合を除き，２つ以上の低い音節で終るということがないようである。…一般に，高いもののあとに低いものがありまた高いものが来ると，前の高いものほど高くは聞こえないということがある（いわゆるdowndrift）ので，ここでは一応X́を高いものとしておく。 [p. 42, note 3]
new_statements.translation: The customary orthography does not mark accent, but here we distinguish by putting ´ over a vowel pronounced high and nothing over a vowel pronounced low. A transcription that abstracts away from accent is shown by underlining. In the accent notation a consonant (or consonant + w/y) is written C, a vowel V, and a preconsonantal nasal N. An arbitrary string of phonemes is written X; X́ means that all the vowels contained in that X are high, and an X with nothing on it means that all its vowels are low. Since N is pronounced high only immediately after a high vowel, ´ is not put on it even when it is pronounced high. [p. 2] ... In general in this language, except in cases like those described for Group A verbs in §2-1-1 to 5, a form does not seem to end in two or more low syllables. ... In general, when a high is followed by a low and then another high, the second high does not sound as high as the preceding one (so-called downdrift), so here X́ is provisionally treated as high. [p. 42, note 3]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for sima1258 and no existing statements were passed in, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict; this work supplies the first statement: the variety is described tonally (H vs L on every vowel) with nothing said about stress. It is the expanded Japanese version of Yukawa 1987 'A Tonological Study of Mwenyi Verbs' (Studies in Zambian Languages 35-72), whose English wording ('´ is put on the high-toned vowel and nothing on the low-toned vowel', printed p. 36) the prior world-store pass already recorded with the same reading; the Japanese version adds §2-7 and the downdrift note. It describes Mwenyi (Simwenyi), which Glottolog lists as dialect mwen1238 under s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yukawa's 'アクセント' here is pitch: every vowel is either high (marked ´) or low, and the whole paper (his own English title: 'A Tentative Tonal Analysis') describes the H/L tone patterns of each verb form, with verbs falling into two tonal groups A and B (e.g. kúmona vs kunyáza type stems) and the tones of subject/object prefixes and tense markers conditioned by neighbouring morphemes. There is no statement about stress, prominence or a fixed accent position at the word level; the words 強勢/ストレス/強弱 do not occur in the text. So the work is a tonal description that is silent on stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress discussed at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Phonetic downdrift (p. 42 n. 3); a preconsonantal nasal is high only right after a high vowel (p. 2); forms generally do not end in two or more low syllables (p. 42 n. 3); the height of some subject prefixes was unstable in the informant's pronunciation (p. 38); several patterns flagged as needing re-checking (notes 4, 7, 8, 11, 19). In §2-7-4 (pp. 27-28) Yukawa doubts that all verb-form tone patterns can be derived from morpheme-inherent tonal features, since the stem+ending tone (CV(N)X́ vs X́CV(N)CV) varies by tense form without a general rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Mwenyi (Simwenyi), spoken around Kalabo, Western Province, Zambia (~6,000 speakers per p. 1), from one week of elicitation with one speaker, Mwangala Simushi, born 1960 in Ikanda village, Kalabo District, resident in Kalabo since age 5, also speaking Lozi and English. Yukawa (p. 1, following Lisimba's A Luyana Dialectology) places Mwenyi among the western dialects of Luyana alongside Liuwa, Makoma, Mashi, Mbukushu, Mulonga, Nyengo and Simaa, i.e. he treats Simaa and Mwenyi as sister varieties, not the same one; Glottolog subsumes Mwenyi as dialect mwen1238 under sima1258, which is why the work is attached to this item. No source on Simaa proper (Nuclear Simaa) was among the listed works.

sources.note: General statement for Zambian Bantu languages, not Simaa-specific (printed p.70, sec. 3.4 Tone and Stress): 'In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed.. In some languages, however, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syllable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force.. stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning.' Simaa is mentioned only in the speaker tables, Fortune's lexicostatistic chart (p.59) and for having dental fricatives (p.68).

sources.note: Nothing. The paper treats Mwenyi (a western Luyana dialect, grouped by Glottolog under Simaa) as a two-tone language: p.36 'Although the convention does not use any tone mark, an acute is put on the high-toned vowel and nothing on the low-toned vowel in this paper'; verbs fall into two tonal groups (A/B) and every tense form is given a H/L tonal representation. No mention of stress, accent placement, penultimate lengthening or prominence anywhere in the 38 pages (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent/penult/promin/length: no hits; intro pp.35-40 and pp.69-72 read in full).
